Fit a factorised hurdle (or zero-inflated) concentration-response model

Source: R/bnec_hurdle.R
bnec_hurdle.Rd

Fits a two-part concentration-response model as a pair of ordinary bnec fits: one for the response of the units that gave a non-zero value, and a bernoulli model for the probability of being non-zero. The two are returned together so that the combined endpoint – the expected response per unit exposed – can be derived from them.

bnec_hurdle(formula, data, model_survival = NULL, family_growth = NULL, ...)

Arguments

formula

Either a character string defining an R formula or an actual formula object. See bayesnecformula. The response must be untransformed, and zero values in it are taken to mean the individual did not survive. A cens() aterm is allowed alongside it; other aterms are refused, see Details.

data

A data.frame containing the data to use with the formula. Every unit that entered the experiment must be present, with 0 recorded for those that gave no response. Rows omitted rather than zeroed cannot be distinguished from ones never run, and would be read as a smaller experiment rather than as zeros.

model_survival

An optional character vector naming the model or model group to use for the survival component. Defaults to whatever crf specifies in formula, i.e. the same set as the response component.

family_growth

A family function for the response of the non-zero subset. Defaults to NULL, in which case it is chosen from that subset the same way bnec would: Gamma for a positive continuous response, Beta for one bounded on (0, 1). A two-block family (hurdle_gamma, zero_inflated_beta) is refused, because bnec_hurdle is itself the two-part model, and so are the zero-inflated count families, which are mixtures rather than hurdles – see bnec. Note that a count family is accepted here but fitted untruncated to the non-zero subset, whereas the positive part of a hurdle on counts is zero-truncated. That overestimates the mean where the mean is small, which is the upper end of the concentration range; a zero-truncated count family is not yet available.

...

Further arguments passed to both bnec calls.

Value

An object of class bayesnechurdlefit.

Details

This covers the zero-inflated case too. brms names the equivalent joint families hurdle_gamma and zero_inflated_beta, but the distinction is nominal: zero-inflation differs from a hurdle only when the base distribution can itself produce zeros, which neither the Gamma nor the Beta can. The Stan density brms generates for zero_inflated_beta is the hurdle form, with no mixture at zero. One function therefore serves both, and the appropriate family is chosen from the data – Gamma for a positive continuous response, Beta for a proportion on (0, 1).

Throughout the documentation the two parts are called "growth" and "survival", after the case they were written for – individuals that die contribute a zero and the survivors contribute a measurement. Nothing in the implementation is specific to that reading: any process producing exact zeros alongside a continuous response fits the same structure. Algal growth rate expressed as a proportion of a ceiling, with replicates that failed entirely, is the same model.

Why two fits rather than one

The hurdle log-likelihood separates exactly into a Bernoulli term over all individuals and a zero-bounded term over the survivors only:


log p(y_i) = log Bernoulli(alive_i | 1 - hu_i)
           + 1[y_i > 0] * log Gamma(y_i | mu_i, shape)

The two blocks share no parameters, so with independent priors the posterior factorises and fitting them separately gives the same inference as fitting them jointly. Doing so also makes the full crossed model comparison tractable: elpd(a, b) = elpd_growth(a) + elpd_survival(b), so all combinations of the two model sets can be compared from the two fits alone rather than by fitting every pair.

The factorisation does not hold if the two components are coupled, for example by a shared group-level effect. Group-level terms supplied here apply within each component independently.

Coding of deaths

A 0 response means the individual did not survive; it is a label, not a measurement. Where mortality is instead recorded by omitting rows, those rows must be reinstated as zeros before calling this function.

Censoring, and which aterms are allowed

cens() is the one aterm accepted on the response. bnec itself carries three – trials(), weights() and cens() – and of those cens() is the only one whose meaning stays unambiguous once the response is split across two models. It is also the one with a use here that nothing else covers. A growth endpoint can be both zero-bounded with structural zeros and left-censored at the recording resolution, and only a two-part model with a censored response component can tell the two apart: a death is a structural zero belonging to the Bernoulli component, while a survivor measured below the limit is a real observation of the growth component whose value is known only to lie at or below a bound.

The declaration is routed accordingly. It is passed through to the growth component, where the censoring indicator travels as an ordinary data column and is subset along with everything else, and it is dropped from the survival component, whose alive/dead response is observed exactly. A row that is both zero and censored is refused rather than assigned to one of them.

Under a Gamma growth component the censoring bound cannot be 0 – bnec rejects that, correctly, because the censored likelihood contribution there is F(0) = 0. The bound has to be the resolution limit, so the encoding is "at most the smallest resolvable value" rather than "at most zero".

The other two are refused by name, with the reason. trials() has no meaning for either component, and weights() is a modelling decision – whether a weight applies to the growth component, the survival component or both – that this function will not make on the user's behalf. Aterms beyond those three are refused here as well, though they would not reach brms in any case: model.frame drops them for an ordinary bnec fit too. Making the two bnec calls directly remains available for anything outside this set.

See also

bnec for the equivalent joint fit via family = "hurdle_gamma" or family = "zero_inflated_beta", bayesnechurdlefit, crossed_weights

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
library(bayesnec)
data(nec_data)
# code a few individuals as having died
nec_data$y[nec_data$x > 2.5] <- 0
fit <- bnec_hurdle(y ~ crf(x, "nec3param"), data = nec_data)
nec(fit)
ecx(fit, ecx_val = 10)
} # }
